# Diagnosing P0305: When a Single Cylinder Misfire Stays Localized

A persistent P0305 code on a 2006 Jetta 2.5L indicates a misfire isolated specifically to cylinder number 5. The fact that you swapped coil packs and the error remained locked to cylinder 5 is a critical diagnostic clue. In modern engine control units (ECUs), swapping ignition components across cylinders is a standard troubleshooting step designed to rule out faulty coils or spark plugs. When this test fails to shift the misfire code, it effectively eliminates those specific hardware items as the root cause for that particular cylinder.

The most probable culprit in this scenario involves the fuel delivery system restricted to that single injector. On many VW/Audi engines of this era, a stuck open fuel injector can flood the combustion chamber with unburnt gasoline. This flooding creates an overly rich mixture that prevents proper ignition, triggering the misfire detection logic. Because the ECU monitors crankshaft rotation variance (often via the Crank Position Sensor or Camshaft sensors), it calculates cylinder-by-cylinder contribution to power output. If cylinder 5 is consistently delivering less effective combustion due to a leaky injector, the code sticks there regardless of which coil pack sits on top of it.

Before moving to invasive disassembly, consider checking for vacuum leaks specific to that cylinder's intake path or inspecting the fuel rail pressure if you have access to a gauge. However, given your history with jump-starting the vehicle, we must address electrical integrity as a secondary possibility. While jumping a car rarely causes direct physical damage to an injector, it can induce voltage spikes that stress ECU output drivers controlling specific cylinders. If the driver circuit for cylinder 5 has degraded internally within the ECU, it might not be sending sufficient ground or power to activate the injector or coil properly under load.

Your update regarding the P0300 code (random/multiple misfire) suggests a potential shift in diagnosis. A P0300 often indicates that the engine management system has detected a misfire frequency across multiple cylinders, which can happen when one cylinder is severely out of sync, causing erratic idle dynamics that ripple through the entire combustion cycle. Alternatively, it could suggest that the initial swap test inadvertently contaminated other cylinders with debris or that a separate issue—such as a vacuum leak introduced during battery disconnection—is now manifesting.

If you lack the tools to remove spark plugs yet, focus on visual inspection of the wiring harness connecting to cylinder 5. Look for cracked insulation, chafed wires against the firewall, or corrosion at the connector pins. A poor electrical connection here can mimic a coil failure but will remain localized even after swapping coils.

In professional environments, technicians might use an oscilloscope to view the injector waveform on cylinder 5 compared to the other four. If the injector is stuck open, you would see a continuous signal without the characteristic "off" pulse needed to stop fuel flow. Alternatively, listening with a mechanic's stethoscope while cranking the engine can reveal if one injector is dripping fuel more audibly than its neighbors.

If diagnostics point toward an internal ECU driver failure or a seized injector that cannot be cleared by cleaning, replacement of those specific components becomes necessary. Given the age of the vehicle and the complexity of the 2.5L engine, professional diagnosis may ultimately provide the most cost-effective route to prevent further damage to the catalytic converter from unburnt fuel.
